summaries.example: Imagine a museum sorting many kinds of festivals, prayers, stories, rules, and ceremonies. One person might group them by belief in spirits. Another might group them by how they bring a community together. A third might include ways of living connected to a big picture of reality. Their shelves would not hold exactly the same things.
summaries.summary: The concept of religion is difficult because the word has changed and is used in several ways. Long ago, its Latin ancestor, religio, could describe carefulness, duty, or devotion. Later, religion became a name for a kind of social formation, including traditions that involve gods, spirits, or other important powers. Some scholars define it by what it refers to, while others define it by what it does, such as joining people into a moral community or guiding their values. Philosophers also disagree about the shape of the category. A monothetic definition looks for a necessary and sufficient feature. A polythetic definition sees a family of overlapping similarities, so some examples may be more typical than others. The entry also explains that the category has been used in colonial and political settings. Critics therefore question whether religion is a natural thing, a useful scholarly tool, or a label that can distort cultures. The main lesson is that defining a familiar word can require history, comparison, and careful attention to who is doing the naming.
key_ideas: The word religion has not always meant the same thing. Its earlier Latin background was connected with careful duty or devotion, not simply a group of beliefs.
Over time, scholars used religion as a broad name for many kinds of social life, including practices connected with gods, spirits, powers, or a larger order of reality.
Some definitions look for one required feature. Other definitions look for overlapping similarities, like members of a family who resemble one another in different ways.
Some scholars ask whether religion names something real in the world. Others stress that the category was shaped by scholars, politics, and European history.
summaries.why_it_matters: Words used to compare cultures can help us notice patterns, but they can also hide important differences or carry older judgments. Thinking carefully about religion can help students listen more fairly when people describe their own lives and traditions. It also shows a wider philosophical lesson: categories such as culture or democracy may have histories and fuzzy boundaries too.

important_terms.definition: A word or idea used to sort several things into one group.
An idea that something must have one special feature, or a fixed set of features, to belong in a group.
An idea that things can belong together because they share several features, even if no single feature is shared by all.
The study of how a word or idea changes as people use it in different times and places.

questions_to_think_about: Can a group belong together even if every member does not share one exact feature?
What might change when people use one word to describe practices from many different cultures?
Should a useful category have sharp edges, or can it have blurry edges?

summaries.example: Suppose a researcher wants to compare Theravada Buddhism, a tradition centered on the Dao, and a community organized around a powerful political ideal. A substantive definition may include the first two if it refers to a distinctive non-empirical reality, while a functional definition might also include the political community if it organizes values and creates solidarity. A monothetic definition must decide whether each case passes a required test. A polythetic definition may treat them as more or less religion-like, depending on the features selected and the threshold used.
summaries.summary: The entry examines religion not as an automatically self-explanatory object but as a contested concept with a changing history. Its Latin predecessor, religio, had senses involving scrupulousness, obligation, and devotion. The modern use of religion as a social genus developed later and was extended across increasingly diverse cases. Substantive definitions identify religion through a distinctive kind of reality, while functional definitions identify a role such as generating social solidarity or organizing ultimate values. The entry then contrasts monothetic and polythetic analyses. Monothetic accounts require necessary and sufficient conditions, producing relatively clear inclusion and exclusion. Polythetic accounts treat cases as a family resemblance group. Bounded versions use a specified feature set and threshold; open versions allow the category to develop as new cases are recognized; anchored versions impose one required feature while retaining graded membership. Finally, reflexive scholarship asks how academic categories are constructed and how the term’s use has been connected with colonial and political projects. Some critics reject religion as an independent referent, while others argue that a constructed scholarly category can still illuminate real social structures. The disagreement is therefore not merely about vocabulary: it concerns reference, history, comparison, and the purposes of inquiry.
key_ideas: The meaning of religion expanded from the Latin religio, associated with scrupulous duty or devotion, to a category for diverse social formations. The entry presents this expansion as moving from theistic, to polytheistic, to broader cosmic criteria.

Definitions may be substantive or functional. Substantive accounts focus on distinctive realities; functional accounts focus on effects such as solidarity or life-orientation. These approaches can classify different cases.

Monothetic accounts seek a yes-or-no boundary through necessary and sufficient conditions. Polythetic accounts reject a single essence and can allow prototypes, borderline cases, and family resemblance.

Polythetic accounts are not all alike. A bounded version fixes a list of features and a threshold; an open version allows the category and its relevant features to evolve; an anchored version requires one feature but not that feature alone to be sufficient.

Reflexive and skeptical approaches emphasize that the category was historically shaped and sometimes used to rank or control cultures. Yet criticism of a concept does not always deny that it refers to real social structures.

A definition cannot be assessed apart from its purpose. A sharp monothetic boundary may help when a yes-or-no decision is needed, while a polythetic account may better represent variation and historical change.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept of religion is a case study in how classification works. A definition can reveal patterns, but it can also impose assumptions from the society that created it. Understanding the difference between lexical and stipulative definitions, between essentialist and family-resemblance models, and between critique and outright nonrealism helps researchers compare cultures without treating their own categories as neutral or timeless.

important_terms.definition: A broad category used for multiple social formations, such as traditions involving worship, spirits, cosmic order, or shared life-guiding commitments.
A definition based on the kind of reality or object a practice concerns, such as spirits, gods, or a non-empirical order.
A definition based on the role a practice plays, such as producing solidarity or organizing a person’s values.
An analysis that uses necessary and sufficient conditions for membership in a category.
An analysis in which cases share overlapping features without one feature being required in every case; it can produce degrees of typicality.
A definition assigned for a particular purpose; it is judged by usefulness and appropriateness rather than simply true or false.
The study of how scholars’ categories are shaped by their own histories, purposes, and social positions.
The view that a social structure may exist and affect people even if they have not named or conceptualized it.

questions_to_think_about: What is gained and lost when religion is defined by a distinctive reality rather than by a social function?
Does a category become unfair because it was historically used for political purposes, or can it be revised and used carefully?
Would an open family-resemblance concept be better for historical comparison than a fixed definition?
Can a social structure be real even when the people involved do not possess the same category for it?

summaries.example: Think about making a club chart. You could say a club counts only if every member votes, pays dues, and attends meetings. That is like a monothetic definition: it uses required rules. Or you could say clubs usually have meetings, shared goals, activities, and a sense of membership, but not every club has all four. That is like a polythetic definition. One club might be a very typical example, while another might be a borderline case.
summaries.summary: The Stanford entry asks a basic but challenging question: what does the word religion pick out? The answer has changed over time. The Latin word from which it developed was linked to careful duty, devotion, and obligation. Later, religion became a general category for different social ways of living. Scholars have tried to define that category in several ways. A substantive definition focuses on a special kind of reality, such as gods, spirits, or a broad order of existence. A functional definition focuses on a job religion performs, such as creating community or organizing a person’s values. These definitions may include different examples. The entry also compares two ways of understanding concepts. Monothetic approaches search for necessary and sufficient conditions, giving a yes-or-no answer. Polythetic approaches use family resemblance: members share some features, but no single feature must appear in every case. Some versions use a fixed list, while others allow the category to change as new cases are recognized. The entry ends by discussing criticism of the category itself. Because the word has been shaped by scholars, colonial encounters, and political judgments, some thinkers question whether it describes a real thing. Others argue that a human-made category can still help us study real social patterns.
key_ideas: The word religion has a history. Its Latin ancestor could mean careful duty or devotion before religion became a broad label for social traditions.
Scholars have proposed different definitions. Some focus on gods, spirits, or a larger reality; others focus on community, values, or the role a tradition plays in life.
A monothetic definition asks whether something meets a required test. A polythetic definition allows clearer examples, less typical examples, and borderline cases.
The category has expanded over time. Definitions that began with one supreme deity were later broadened to include many gods, spirits, and non-personal cosmic orders.
Some scholars argue that religion is a useful way to describe real social patterns. Others say the category was created for particular historical and political purposes and can mislead us.
There is no single agreed answer about whether religion has an essence. The best definition may depend partly on what a researcher is trying to study.
summaries.why_it_matters: Learning how the concept of religion works teaches a broader skill: examine labels before treating them as natural facts. This is especially important when comparing cultures. A label may help organize information, but responsible thinking requires asking about its history, its limits, and the purpose for which it is being used.

important_terms.definition: A general group or kind that contains several different examples.
A definition that identifies religion by what kind of reality it involves, such as gods, spirits, or a cosmic order.
A definition that identifies religion by what it does, such as bringing people together or guiding their priorities.
An approach that looks for a required feature or required set of features shared by every member.
An approach that groups cases through several overlapping features instead of one shared essence.
A pattern in which things belong together because they resemble one another in different, overlapping ways.
A careful examination of the categories and assumptions used by scholars themselves.

questions_to_think_about: Why might one scholar include a tradition that another scholar leaves out?
Is a blurry category always a bad category?
How could a label created in one historical setting affect the people to whom it is applied?
When would a yes-or-no definition be more useful than a family-resemblance definition?
